source.title: Minimum Lines to Represent a Line Chart

teaching.hint: At which intermediate points is ending one straight segment unavoidable?

solution_outline.decisive_insight: Every change in consecutive direction forces a boundary; maximal collinear runs each need and suffice with one segment.
solution_outline.approach: Sort points by day. Compare consecutive displacement directions using exact cross products or normalized integer ratios, and count a first segment plus every direction change.
solution_outline.state_and_invariant: The prior direction is that of the preceding elementary segment; the running count is the number of maximal equal-direction runs processed.
solution_outline.correctness: Two adjacent elementary segments can be one straight segment exactly when their slopes agree. A slope change cannot be covered by a single straight segment, supplying a necessary boundary. Combining each maximal equal-slope run attains those boundaries, so their count is minimal.
solution_outline.complexity: O(n log n) time and O(log n) auxiliary sorting stack space with cross-product comparisons after in-place sorting.
solution_outline.pitfall: Floating-point slopes can misclassify near-equal ratios; cross-product multiplication must handle values near 10^18.

common_wrong_turns: Floating-point slopes can misclassify near-equal ratios; cross-product multiplication must handle values near 10^18.
source_fidelity_notes: Clarified finite connected segment counting rather than distinct infinite lines, chronological order, and the single-point case; introductory exact-geometry role.
